claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy nanoscale multilayers is governed by a two-stage mechanism.
The FCC layers are more ductile than the BCC layers.
The first deformation stage consists of dislocation buildup within the FCC layers.
The second deformation stage consists of shear yielding at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Severe lattice distortion and local short-range order at FCC/BCC interfaces mediate interface shear yielding.
The as-deposited coating has relatively uniform nanoscale layer thickness and minimal preexisting interfacial defects.
Controlled deposition conditions can systematically modify lattice mismatch or short-range order at the interfaces.
Interfacial lattice distortion and short-range order modulate strain transfer and dislocation motion between FCC and BCC layers.
Increasing strain causes the compositionally complex interfaces to yield by shear.
Interface shear yielding accelerates plastic flow.
The proposed two-stage process retards immediate catastrophic deformation.
Sustained loading will produce an initial gradual creep stage followed by accelerated deformation after interface yielding begins.
The initial creep stage will be accompanied by dislocation pile-ups in the FCC layers.
The accelerated stage will be accompanied by interfacial shear bands or disrupted interfacial ordering.
The mechanism applies only while layer thickness remains nanoscale and loading avoids delamination and phase transformation.
Changing interfacial characteristics should measurably change the two-stage creep response and associated microstructural evolution.
Failure of interface modification to change the creep transition, dislocation behavior, or interface disruption would falsify the proposed two-stage mechanism.
